name: Makwe
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Devos, Maud. 2014. Melodic H in Makwe. Africana Linguistica 20: 81-99. DOI 10.3406/aflin.2014.1025 (Persée, open access; text saved from Persée's per-page content endpoints)
catalog_locator: p. 82, Section 2 'Background and complications' and Section 2.1 'Verb-final H tones and phonological phrasing' (Persee page block whose header reads '82 Africana Linguistica 20 (2014)')
catalog_quote: The tone bearing unit in Makwe is the mora. Each mora has a definite value for tone, i. e. either H or L. Contour tones (falling and rising) are only found on dimoraic syllables in the penult of a phonological phrase and are analysed as combinations of H and L tones. Tone assignment as well as tone processes can be described by referring to H tones only. There is no evidence of downstep in Makwe, and when two H tones come together, they fuse (or a H deletes). As is the case for most zone P Bantu languages, Makwe has a predictable verb tone system (Odden 2003: 534‑535). It lacks lexical tone in verb stems. Instead, melodic H patterns (no melodic H, SF, S1& SF, PU, S1) are assigned to the verb stem on the basis of verb tense. [...] As is true for many Eastern and Southern Bantu languages (Hyman 2013), Makwe does not have lexical vowel length but does attest penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of a phonological phrase. A word‑final H tone that occurs in phrase‑final position regularly retracts to the second mora of the lengthened penultimate syllable, as is the case with the final H tone of the Imperative in (1a). When the same verb‑final H tone occurs in phrase‑medial position, it regularly shifts to the first mora of the following noun where it is subject to regular tone spreading processes, as in (1b).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makwe is a two-tone (H/L) mora-counting tone language; verbs carry no lexical tone but receive tense-determined melodic H tones (stem-final, stem-initial, penult, or initial+final). The only prominence-like property described is automatic penultimate lengthening at the end of the phonological phrase (there is no lexical vowel length), which also attracts phrase-final H tones (retraction to the lengthened penult). The source never uses the term 'stress' and makes no statement of word stress; no explicit 'no stress' claim either.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic stems: a final H fails to retract to the penult in some tenses (Subjunctive, p. 83); some enclitics lengthen a preceding vowel (Devos 2013, fn. 10, citing Makwe).
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase level: lengthening (and H retraction to the penult) is stated for the end of the phonological phrase, not the word; conjoint verb forms phrase with the following noun and then show neither lengthening nor retraction (p. 82-83). The primary grammar (Devos 2008: 32-33, phonology ch. pp. 14-40) was not accessible and should be checked for any explicit remark on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Devos describes the Makwe of Palma district, Cabo Delgado, Mozambique (title of the grammar: 'A Grammar of Makwe (Palma; Mozambique)'); this is Glottolog makw1236 (ISO ymk), Guthrie G402 (earlier P.231). Devos 2014 (p. 82) characterizes Makwe as 'the outcome of a contact situation between a variant of Swahili (G42) and a variant of Makonde (P23)'. No dialect subdivision is at issue.

sources.note: Never uses the word 'stress'. p. 82: TBU is the mora; every mora is H or L; contour tones only on dimoraic syllables in the penult of a phonological phrase; no downstep; verbs have no lexical tone (melodic H by tense: SF, S1&SF, PU, S1); 'Makwe does not have lexical vowel length but does attest penultimate lengthening (PUL) at the end of a phonological phrase'; a phrase-final word-final H retracts to the second mora of the lengthened penult.

sources.citation: Devos, Maud. 2013. Vowel length in Shangaci: when lexical vowel length and penultimate lengthening co-occur. Africana Linguistica 19: 85-107. (Persée, open access)
sources.note: About Shangaci, but reports Makwe second-hand from her own grammar: 'Such is the case for Makwe (Devos 2008: 32-33), where any long vowel marks the end of a phonological phrase' and 'a language like Makwe where vowel length exists always and only in the phrasal penult syllable (Devos 2008: 32-33)'; generic remark that 'penult stress is a widespread phenomenon in Bantu languages and its most common phonetic correlate is vowel lengthening' (citing Downing 2004, Hyman 2009) — not applied to Makwe by name.
Nothing on phonology or stress; only cites Devos 2008 and the Swahili-Makonde mixed-language suggestion (Arends et al. 1995).

sources.citation: Odden, David & Lee Bickmore. 2014. Melodic tone in Bantu: overview. Africana Linguistica 20: 3-13. (Persée, open access)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; notes that in Makwe (Devos) the one to three tones of a verbal melody link to the penult and that a penultimate pattern can combine with a stem-initial H.

sources.note: This work describes Bantu cross-linguistic survey of penultimate lengthening (Appendices 1-3 list 59 languages with revised Guthrie codes; Makwe is not among them and is not named anywhere in the text). The work never mentions Makwe (no alternate name or P2x code other than P23 Makonde appears). Nothing here bears on the catalog's tonal / lexical-tone coding for Makwe (Devos 2014). Do not use this work as a Makwe source; it is a Bantu-wide survey.
